column19: With our department having approximately 130 individual services, this new process has been extremely time-consuming, taxing, and frustrating.  The template is very finicky and required many additional hours for data entry as we could not simply copy and paste from previous or existing in-house workbooks. The process for requesting new SIDs and STIDs was laborious and frustrating, certainly not easy or accurate.  We also spent many additional hours correcting system-generated errors when it issued (sometimes repeatedly) false or duplicate SIDs or STDs. This new process has also caused a rift in collaboration between the Service and Security divisions within our department who now must work separately to complete similar work related to critical services and the Service Inventory.  In discussions with our Security counterparts, their side of the service inventory work (critical services) lacks support and clear direction -- our colleagues leaned heavily on our Service team to provide guidance and training on how to use GCEPM (formerly used for Service Inventory as Clarity) as they felt they did not receive adequate training or direction from TBS Security section. This has added additional stress to our Service workload that should be innovative instead of regressive in both process and reporting tools. The messaging and direction to our two divisions varied and caused a lot of confusion within the department. The Clarity tool and former reporting process is favoured by our team in comparison to the most recent year's.

Key Areas for Consideration
1. Service Inventory Reporting Requirements
•	The introduction of new fields (e.g., ‘Automated Decision-Making’ and ‘Program ID Code’) brought some challenges in ensuring accurate completion.
•	Certain definitions, such as "Is the service supported by automated decision-making," could benefit from greater clarity to facilitate consistent interpretation across departments.
•	Multiple updates to reporting requirements this year necessitated repeated adjustments, resulting in a time-consuming and intensive process.
2. Service Inventory Process and the New Template
•	The new template was provided later than in previous years, which made it difficult to integrate into existing workflows.
•	Mid-cycle modifications to the template resulted in inconsistencies and required additional rework.
•	The template’s format, particularly the lack of pre-populated data, increased manual effort and complexity.
•	Given these challenges, ESDC had to rely on its previous template and manually align the data, which significantly increased workload.
•	We don’t think that backlogs information should have been removed from the template.
•	We don’t think that the last year for review of service standards should have been removed from the template. 
3. Transition to the Open Government Portal
•	While the transition was intended to streamline the process, it introduced additional complexity, requiring time and technical knowledge to navigate.
•	Questions related to registration and account setup had to be addressed by a separate TBS team, which led to confusion.
•	A technical issue caused by the transition to Open Gov prevented our Inventory from being uploaded by the November 30 deadline, putting our submission at risk.
•	There should have been more testing with departments or a pilot. 
4. TBS List of Reporting Issues (critical and minor)
•	Many of the flagged errors stemmed from the limitations of the quality control script, which does not account for contextual explanations provided in non-standard responses.
•	Of the 29 reporting issues ESDC received, the majority were minor technical issues rather than substantive errors.
•	In some cases, flagged errors related to application volume reporting were not applicable to certain services, highlighting the need for a broader metric that captures the full scope of service interactions.
•	However, the most recent issue with Program ID codes reveled some errors in the Inventory that we were unaware of. Since the request to add a program ID code was new, and our templates were not pre-populated, we were unsure whether we had selected the correct program codes. It was only after receiving a message from TBS that we realized we had used the wrong ID code for a new service. As a result, we reached out to find a responsible Branch within ESDC to review and validate all program codes to identify any potential mistakes which, as it turned out, we had made.
To help improve the Service Inventory process in the future, we would like to share the following recommendations for your consideration:
•	Providing the Service Inventory reporting requirements and updated templates by May each year would allow departments sufficient time for adjustments and the implementation of new requirements.
•	The template should be pre-populated with previous submissions to minimize manual entry and the risk of errors. It should also allow for flexible data entry, including non-standard responses.
•	Departments should have sufficient time to test new platforms and templates before the final submission deadline. A pilot testing phase could help in identifying potential issues early.
•	The system should flag errors immediately during data entry would help prevent last-minute corrections.
•	TBS should reconsider the restriction of volumetric reporting to "applications" and introduce a broader metric that reflects the full scope of service delivery activities.
•	When transitioning from one platform or the system (e.g. GC EPM to Open Government Portal) a comprehensive training and guidance would help departments adapt efficiently.
We recognize the complexities involved in refining the Service Inventory process and appreciate the steps TBS has already taken to improve it. We hope these suggestions will contribute to a more streamlined and user-friendly experience moving forward.
Thank you for your time and consideration. We look forward to continued collaboration on these improvements.
